```ts
/** Smallest signed margin of any box to the safe zone's edges. */
export declare function checkSafeZone(boxes: Box[], options?: { zone?: Box }): CheckResult;
/** 1 minus the relative aspect error of a delivered size. */
export declare function checkAspect(width: number, height: number, aspect: number, options?: { tolerance?: number }): CheckResult;
/** Signed margin of a duration to `[min, max]`, in seconds. */
export declare function checkDuration(seconds: number, options?: { min?: number; max?: number }): CheckResult;
/** Signed margin of a detector count to `[min, max]`. */
export declare function checkCount(count: number, options?: { min?: number; max?: number }): CheckResult;
/** Share of opaque pixels within `maxDeltaE` (OKLab) of a palette color. */
export declare function checkPalette(
    pixels: Uint8ClampedArray | Uint8Array,
    width: number,
    height: number,
    palette: RGB[],
    options?: { maxDeltaE?: number; minCoverage?: number },
): CheckResult;
/** Share of cuts within `tolerance` seconds of a beat. */
export declare function checkCutAlignment(cuts: number[], beats: number[], options?: { tolerance?: number; minHitRate?: number }): CheckResult;
/** Passes only if every check passes. */
export declare function summarizeChecks(results: CheckResult[]): { pass: boolean; failed: CheckResult['check'][]; minConfidence: number; costMs: number };
```

## Guides

<!-- docs/README.md -->

### Builder guides

Build a focused creative tool, remix an existing agent, or embed a reviewed runtime in your own application. OptimAI Creative Agents is an MIT-licensed SDK with a public source repository; you can use it without the OptimAI Studio application.

Start with a **recipe** when an existing template already does the job. A recipe is JSON containing a reviewed template ID, approved setting values and a creative brief. It can be validated, shared as a file and imported by a compatible host. A **runtime contribution** adds the implementation for a new operation and needs source review, tests and a host release.

#### Choose a starting point

| Goal | Guide | What you will finish with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choose a capability | [Agent catalog](docs/catalog.md) | All 39 templates, their execution paths and actual outputs |
| Create your first recipe | [Quickstart](docs/quickstart.md) | A validated manga-planning recipe and its prepared prompt, with no model required |
| Run a browser tool or add optional local AI | [Runtime guide](docs/runtimes.md) | The correct API, requirements and output for each runtime |
| Try every canvas and vision agent in a browser | [Agent Playground](examples/playground/README.md) | Forms built from the catalog, real runs, share links |
| Start a small app of your own | [Starter kits](docs/quickstart.md#start-an-app-from-a-starter-kit) | A runnable poster app, music visualizer, camera filter or MCP server in `apps/` |
| Embed recipes in your own application | [Host integration](docs/host-integration.md) | Validation, reviewed dispatch, selected inputs and portable export |
| Connect an MCP client | [MCP adapter](docs/mcp.md) | A local stdio server that prepares recipes and can explicitly run local writing |
| Share your work or contribute it upstream | [Release and review](docs/release-and-feature.md) | Reproducible examples and a reviewable pull request |
| Let an AI coding assistant build a recipe | [Recipe skill](skills/build-a-recipe/SKILL.md) | An Agent Skill it can load, plus [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt) with every declaration inlined |
| Implement a new capability | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md#new-reviewed-operations) | Source, declarations, contract updates and meaningful tests |

#### What runs today

The catalog contains 39 reviewed templates: 11 canvas, 3 browser vision, 5 writing, 6 interactive (3D, camera, music and frames) and 14 guided entries (12 workflows and two sketches). Canvas tools export still-image PNGs. Vision, camera tracking and browser writing use the selected-agent setup policy: supported devices prepare reviewed models automatically; Data Saver and constrained connections offer manual setup; writing can also use an eligible model already installed in a local Ollama service. A guided workflow prepares a brief rather than generating its final media.

The core manifest, canvas and Ollama SDKs use no package dependencies. Browser writing, vision and 3D use pinned optional dependencies installed by the host. The real 3D scene, camera effects, face worker and avatar renderers are public modules shared with Studio. The package has no Studio account system, billing, project database or private asset library.

Clone [OptimaiNetwork/optimai-creative-agents](https://github.com/OptimaiNetwork/optimai-creative-agents) and follow the quickstart with Node.js 20 or newer. The source is public; `private: true` in `package.json` currently prevents npm publication. Use the checkout directly or install it from a local path as described in the [main README](README.md).

#### Share locally, contribute publicly

Recipe files and public source contributions are available now. A compatible host, including OptimAI Studio's **Saved** library, can import and export recipe JSON. Studio saves that library in the browser and account scope; export your recipes before moving devices or clearing browser storage.

A public community catalog submission service and applications for featured placement have not launched. Opening a pull request proposes a source change; importing a file saves a local recipe. Neither action creates a catalog listing or guarantees featuring. The [release guide](docs/release-and-feature.md) explains those boundaries and the material to prepare for review.

#### Reuse an interactive engine

The [interactive host example](examples/interactive/README.md) runs procedural 3D scenes, local camera filters and face-driven original avatars from the public engine modules. It serves pinned dependency code and WASM from the host’s own origin. Model setup is separate from camera permission and publishing; the SDK has no account, billing or project service.

<!-- docs/quickstart.md -->

### Create your first recipe

This guide creates **Cloud Companion**, a manga-planning recipe based on the reviewed **Story Seed** template. You will scaffold it, customize its settings, validate it and prepare a prompt locally. Those steps need no account, API key, model or dependency installation. Optional writing inference produces a written treatment; rendering a manga remains a separate production step.

#### 1. Clone the public repository

Install Node.js 20 or newer and Git, then run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/OptimaiNetwork/optimai-creative-agents.git
cd optimai-creative-agents
node --version
npm run verify
```

Verification should begin with `Validated 39 reviewed agent templates.` and list each template's actual capability. These commands run from the repository root throughout this guide. You do not need the Studio source repository. The package is not currently published to npm; `npm install @optimai/creative-agents` is not the onboarding path.

#### 2. Scaffold Cloud Companion

```sh
npm run create -- cloud-companion --template story-seed
```

The command creates `agents/cloud-companion/agent.json` and `agents/cloud-companion/README.md`. It refuses to overwrite an existing directory. On a repeat run, choose a fresh lowercase slug and use that ID and path throughout the guide. Omitting `--template` selects `story-seed` by default.

Replace the contents of `agents/cloud-companion/agent.json` with:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "1.0",
  "id": "cloud-companion",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "title": "Cloud Companion",
  "description": "Plan a gentle manga adventure about finding courage with a friend.",
  "category": "writing",
  "license": "MIT",
  "capabilities": {
    "network": "none",
    "execution": "declarative",
    "dataAccess": "selected-inputs"
  },
  "recipe": {
    "templateId": "story-seed",
    "values": {
      "form": "manga",
      "style": "manga",
      "audience": "all ages"
    },
    "brief": "A young explorer helps a lost cloud find its way home. Preserve the manga art direction, give the pair a clear shared goal, and end with a small act of courage."
  }
}
```

`templateId` selects an existing implementation. `values` overrides its declared defaults, and `brief` supplies creative direction. Change the title, description and brief to make your own recipe. Keep the category consistent with the template and the v1 capability values as shown.

To discover supported settings before editing:

```sh
node --input-type=module -e 'import { getAgentTemplate } from "./src/index.mjs"; console.log(JSON.stringify(getAgentTemplate("story-seed").fields, null, 2));'
```

The [manifest schema](schema/agent-manifest.schema.json) is useful for editor validation. The runtime validator also checks the selected template's fields. Unknown settings, unsupported select values and extra properties are errors. Author/contact details and repository links belong in the README; executable scripts, model endpoints and credentials do not belong in the manifest.

#### 3. Validate and prepare the prompt

```sh
node scripts/verify.mjs agents/cloud-companion/agent.json
```

Expected output: `Validated cloud-companion (story-seed).`

Run this complete command to read your recipe and print its prepared prompt:

```sh
node --input-type=module <<'JS'
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { validateAgentManifest, compileAgentPrompt } from './src/index.mjs';

const source = JSON.parse(await readFile('agents/cloud-companion/agent.json', 'utf8'));
const result = validateAgentManifest(source);
if (!result.success) throw new Error(result.errors.join('\n'));
console.log(compileAgentPrompt(result.manifest));
JS
```

The output names **Story Seed**, includes manga direction, the audience and your cloud-adventure brief, and describes the eventual Story Studio handoff. It prepares text; it does not invoke a model or generate artwork. You have now completed a working recipe authoring flow.

Check the package before contributing changes:

```sh
npm test
npm run verify
```

The tests use controlled fixtures and a local mock provider; they need no paid service or downloaded model. CLI and MCP integration tests start a temporary loopback listener, so a restricted sandbox must permit that listener. Manifest validation checks your recipe's contract; package tests check SDK behavior. Review actual creative output separately when you run a writer.

#### 4. Use the recipe

**In your own host:** validate the JSON, choose the reviewed runtime and supply only selected inputs. [Host integration](docs/host-integration.md) covers this boundary; the [runtime guide](docs/runtimes.md) covers execution. For a first browser integration without AI downloads, try the [browser example](examples/browser):

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1
```

From the repository root, this serves the example at [http://127.0.0.1:8080/examples/browser/](http://127.0.0.1:8080/examples/browser/). Python 3 is needed only for this optional static server. Open the page in a browser, use the sample artwork or choose your own image, then preview and export a PNG. The example demonstrates the canvas SDK; Story Seed uses a writing runtime instead.

**In OptimAI Studio:** open **AI Agents → Saved → Import agent**, select `agents/cloud-companion/agent.json`, then open Cloud Companion. Choose a supported browser writing model or an eligible installed local Ollama model through the workspace controls and review the written result. Continue to Story Studio as a separate action when you want production. The recipe JSON alone does not download a model or authorize spending.

Saved recipes stay in this browser and account scope. Use **Export agent manifest** to keep a portable copy before clearing browser storage or moving devices. Importing or exporting does not publish a community listing.

**From the CLI, optionally:** start your own Ollama service and install a supported model outside this kit. Replace `installed-model` with its exact installed name:

```sh
node scripts/run.mjs --manifest agents/cloud-companion/agent.json --model installed-model
```

The default endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:11434`. The SDK checks installed model metadata, requests a structured document and validates its output, with one bounded repair attempt. It prints the written artifact as JSON; Ctrl+C cancels the request. It never installs a model or falls back to a cloud provider. See the [runtime guide](docs/runtimes.md) for eligibility, limits and host configuration.

#### Start an app from a starter kit

A recipe is data; a starter kit is a small app you own. Each kit is a folder of plain files that imports the SDK by package name (`@optimai/creative-agents/canvas-lab` and so on):

```sh
npm run create -- --kits                         # list the kits
npm run create -- my-poster --kit poster-app     # creates apps/my-poster/
python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:8080/apps/my-poster/](http://127.0.0.1:8080/apps/my-poster/) and click **Make poster**. Leave out the name (`npm run create -- --kit poster-app`) to use the kit's own name. The command never overwrites an existing folder.

| Kit | Runs in | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `poster-app` | Browser | A poster maker: a form drawn from the Poster Lab schema, an on-device render, alt text and a PNG download |
| `music-visualizer` | Browser | A song from your device drives four music-reactive looks, a flash-limited beat pulse and a cover export |
| `camera-filter` | Browser | Live camera effects from the Camera Stage recipe, a photo fallback and snapshots |
| `mcp-creative-server` | Node.js | Your own stdio MCP server offering the agents you choose as read-only recipe tools |

Browser kits carry an import map that points at this checkout, so they run with no install or bundler. To move one into Vite, Next.js or another bundler, run `npm install` in the kit (its only dependency is a `file:` link to this folder, so nothing is downloaded), delete the import map and keep the imports. The MCP kit needs `npm install` once, then `npm start`; see its README for client configuration. Every kit's README explains what to change first.

#### 5. Share or contribute

You can share `agent.json` with anyone using a compatible host. Add reproducible input and expected-behavior notes to the generated README so another builder can assess the result. For an upstream change, fork the [public repository](https://github.com/OptimaiNetwork/optimai-creative-agents), work on a branch, run the checks and open a pull request against `main` following [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

A recipe contribution reuses an existing runtime. A new renderer, model or operation requires reviewed SDK source and a host integration; a new JSON field or template ID cannot install it. Public catalog acceptance and editorial featuring are separate processes that have not launched. See [release and review](docs/release-and-feature.md).

<!-- docs/catalog.md -->

### Agent catalog

Choose a template by the result its reviewed implementation produces. The current catalog has **39 templates: 11 canvas, 3 browser vision, 5 writing, 6 interactive and 14 guided entries**. Every template can prepare a prompt; execution uses the runtime listed below.

These groups follow each template's versioned `workspace` descriptor. The SDK exposes `getAgentWorkspace(id)` for dispatch, `getAgentInputPolicy(id)` for file limits, accepted types and browser needs, and derives `CANVAS_LAB_AGENTS` from the same catalog. The two sketch workspaces include browser drawing before guided production; the other 12 guided templates prepare direction directly. Display categories and legacy `runtime` and `executionKind` metadata remain compatible with older recipes. Hosts maintain their own supported-operation allowlist as described in [host integration](docs/host-integration.md).

#### Canvas tools

These 10 tools render selected images or text into still-image PNGs in the browser. They need no model, API key or external dependency. Use `runLocalTool` for the original image operations and `runCanvasLab` for the additional compositions; see [canvas APIs and settings](docs/runtimes.md#canvas-processing).

| Agent | Template ID | Reviewed operation | Actual result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mockup Maker | `mockup-maker` | `image-resize` or `mockup` | Resize/crop one image, or place it in a phone, desktop or gallery frame; PNG |
| Image Finish | `image-finish` | `image-filter` | Color finish on one image with adjustable intensity; PNG |
| Image Grid | `image-grid` | `image-grid` | Contact sheet containing up to eight images; PNG |
| Title Frame | `title-frame` | `type-overlay` | Plain-text title on one still image; PNG |
| Reference Blend | `reference-blend` | `blend` | Two images composited at a selected blend percentage; PNG |
| Pixel Layout | `pixel-layout` | `bento` | Static hero-and-details layout containing up to eight images; PNG |
| Poster Lab | `poster-lab` | `poster` | Title artboard with an optional background image; PNG |
| Transition Lab | `transition-lab` | `transition` | A still frame of a wipe, iris, light-key or push between exactly two images at a selected time, plus a strip of the whole move; PNG |
| Glitch Cut | `glitch-cut` | `glitch` | A seeded glitch (shifted bands and blocks, colour trails or echoes, RGB split and scanlines) on one still image; the same seed redraws it exactly; PNG |
| Print Shop | `print-shop` | `print` | A riso duotone, halftone dots or a Floyd–Steinberg, Bayer or blue-noise dither of one still image on warm paper; the seed redraws the same grain; PNG |
| Letter Pose | `letter-pose` | `letter` | Typographic artboard with an optional background image; PNG |

Inputs must be selected PNG, JPEG or WebP files, each at most 20 MiB and 4096 pixels per side. The original image processors enforce a 16-million-pixel budget for retained images and output; compositions validate each input through that processor and enforce a shared budget for normalized inputs. Compositions have a 1200-pixel output width and ratios of 1:1, 4:5, 16:9 or 9:16. Exported PNGs are limited to 20 MiB.

Canvas tools render supplied artwork and text. A blend preview is not a synthesized scene, and a static layout or transition preview is not an encoded video. Mockup Maker's two operations are alternative host workspaces, counted as one template.

Use `canvasLabRecipeSettings(id, values)` to normalize recipe fields into direct composition settings. Canonical `ratio`, `treatment`, `title`, `color`, `amount` and `mix` settings take precedence over saved legacy aliases when explicitly supplied. Old `format`, `text`, `style`, `intensity` and bento layout fields remain accepted; no saved v1 field is removed. Try the [browser example](examples/browser/README.md) for a complete image resize/filter workflow.

#### Browser vision

These three tools analyze one selected still image using a fixed reviewed MediaPipe model. The host installs the pinned optional dependency, serves a reviewed local worker and WASM assets, and applies the selected-agent model setup policy. See [browser vision setup](docs/runtimes.md#browser-vision).

| Agent | Template ID | Reviewed operation | Actual result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Select & Replace | `select-and-replace` | `person-cutout` | Person cutout with a transparent or solid-color background; PNG and segmentation analysis |
| Motion Pose | `motion-pose` | `pose-reference` | Pose overlay for one person with 33 body landmarks; PNG and landmark analysis |
| Face Performance | `face-performance` | `face-reference` | Face overlay with 478 landmarks and raw blendshape coefficients; PNG and analysis |

Person Cutout uses Selfie Segmenter (249,537 bytes); Motion Pose uses Pose Landmarker Lite (5,777,746 bytes); Face Performance uses Face Landmarker (3,758,596 bytes). Downloads use fixed URLs, exact byte lengths and SHA-256 verification. Running a tool does not download its model implicitly.

Image inputs share the 20 MiB, 4096-pixel-per-side and 16-million-pixel limits. Analysis and PNG output are scaled to at most 1600 pixels per side. Inference uses a local CPU WASM worker with a 60-second timeout and cancellation. Detection quality depends on visibility, lighting and occlusion; missing subjects produce an error.

Select & Replace's local implementation segments people rather than performing arbitrary regional replacement. Motion Pose produces a still reference rather than animation or measured body distances. Face Performance provides geometry and raw rig coefficients; it does not identify people, infer emotions or personality, or swap faces. The templates can also prepare direction for a separate host workflow.

#### Writing agents

These five templates generate validated written artifacts through either the [browser writing runtime](docs/runtimes.md#browser-writing) or [local Ollama writing](docs/runtimes.md#local-ollama-writing). Browser writing needs supported WebGPU hardware, a locally bundled worker and reviewed fixed-model setup; the host may start preparation when the selected-agent policy permits. Ollama writing needs a running loopback service and an explicitly selected eligible installed model.

| Agent | Template ID | Actual written result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast Notes | `cast-notes` | Character identity, motivation, strengths and limits, arc and consistency notes |
| Style Brief | `style-brief` | Art direction, palette, line/material treatment, lighting, composition and things to avoid |
| Storyboard Builder | `storyboard-builder` | 2–12 sequential scene plans with purpose, action, visual treatment, framing, dialogue and sound |
| Prompt Branches | `prompt-branches` | 2–6 creative directions with a shared premise, complete prompt and explanation of each difference |
| Story Seed | `story-seed` | Premise, cast, setting, chapter outline and visual/production direction |

The result includes a title, summary, sections and a prompt to review before a production handoff. It is text; creating illustrations, video or a finished project requires the destination host. Browser briefs are limited to 2,000 characters with a 2,048-token output budget; the manifest contract permits briefs up to 4,000 characters. Start with the three-scene storyboard default for a short draft.

The runtimes validate structure and task-specific content, allow one bounded repair attempt and report failure when the model still returns invalid output. Model choice and hardware affect speed and creative quality. Review the result before using it for production. Recipe preparation with `compileAgentPrompt` works without a model, as shown in the [quickstart](docs/quickstart.md).

#### Interactive 3D, camera, avatars, music and frames

These six templates use shared public engines rather than preparing direction alone. A host owns the interface and its camera permission, recording, selected input and export actions. See the [interactive runtime guide](docs/runtimes.md#interactive-3d-scenes) and [runnable host example](examples/interactive/README.md).

| Agent | Template ID | Workspace | Actual result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model Turntable | `model-turntable` | `3d:scene` | Original procedural subjects or a self-contained static GLB; orbit, camera/lens, material and light controls; PNG and scene recipe |
| Scene Lighting | `scene-lighting` | `3d:scene` | Architectural scene with adjustable key light, atmosphere and camera framing; same real scene engine |
| Camera Stage | `camera-stage` | `camera:effects` | Local webcam or selected image/video filters, with optional tracked halo; canvas output |
| Avatar Stage | `avatar-stage` | `camera:avatar` | Original procedural 3D avatar driven by local face geometry/blendshapes, or an animated demo |
| Sound Canvas | `music-reactive` | `music:reactive` | Four original looks driven by a selected song's analyser data; still PNG or host-recorded visualizer |
| Frame Sculpture | `frame-sculpture` | `frame:sculpture` | Real frames sampled from a short local clip, arranged as an interactive 2.5D sculpture; PNG, turntable video and composition record |

`scene3DRecipeSettings(id, values)` maps `demo`, `lighting`, `finish`, `view`, lens and exposure into actual engine settings. `cameraRecipeSettings(id, values)` maps effect, look, intensity and mirror controls. Neither recipe can provide a model URL, decoder, renderer script or worker path. Three.js is an optional pinned peer. Face tracking reuses the pinned, verified Face Landmarker in a local CPU worker; basic filters and the avatar demo work without a downloaded face model.

GLB imports are limited to 20 MiB, 300,000 visible vertices, 128 primitive parts and 256 nodes, with one embedded static scene. Textures must be embedded PNG/JPEG, no larger than 4096 pixels per side or 16 megapixels total. External/data URLs, compressed decoders, skins, morph targets, instancing and animations are rejected. This is a scene visualizer and composition reference, not generative 3D reconstruction. Avatars are original characters, not identity swaps or emotion classifications.

#### Guided workflows

These 14 templates prepare a bounded prompt and a named Studio destination. The SDK does not process their selected media or execute the production step. A host must implement that workflow and handle any generation, editing, cost confirmation, project persistence or publishing. Use `compileAgentPrompt` to prepare direction and [host integration](docs/host-integration.md) to design the handoff.

| Agent | Template ID | Prepared direction | Destination |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sketch to Scene | `sketch-to-scene` | Develop a selected sketch while preserving composition and shapes | Image Studio |
| World Finder | `world-finder` | Setting, time, atmosphere and coherent visual-world direction | Image Studio |
| Shot Atlas | `shot-atlas` | Alternate camera shots and lens treatment for a selected subject | Image Studio |
| Motion Finish | `motion-finish` | Effect treatment and strength for a clip | Editor Studio |
| Sketch to Motion | `sketch-to-motion` | Action and camera direction for animating a selected sketch | Video Studio |
| Dream Signal | `dream-signal` | Surreal motifs, mood and camera direction | Video Studio |
| Frame Fit | `frame-fit` | Aspect-ratio and framing instructions for selected clips | Editor Studio |
| Rough Cut | `rough-cut` | Structure and pace for a first edit of selected footage | Editor Studio |
| Rhythm Cut | `rhythm-cut` | Rhythm and fragment-length direction for an edit | Editor Studio |
| Frame Study | `frame-study` | Instructions for studying composition, lighting, depth and framing | Image Studio |
| Motion Tracker | `motion-tracker` | Subject and overlay instructions for a tracking workflow | Editor Studio |
| Depth Motion | `depth-motion` | Layered-depth movement and camera direction for a still | Video Studio |
| Scene Scout | `scene-scout` | Location and time-of-day direction for exploring scene angles | Image Studio |
| Scene Remix | `scene-remix` | Setting and visual direction for recomposing a selected subject | Image Studio |

A successful prompt preparation confirms valid recipe data; it is not evidence of completed rendering, tracking, depth reconstruction, video resizing or export. Interactive camera and 3D capabilities are listed separately below. They have real public engines; guided templates still require their destination host.

#### Inspect and remix a template

From the repository root, use `npm run verify` to list current capabilities. Read a template's actual fields before choosing settings (`getAgentFormSchema(id)` from `form-schema` gives the same fields as JSON Schema with control and role hints):

```sh
node --input-type=module -e 'import { getAgentTemplate } from "./src/index.mjs"; console.log(JSON.stringify(getAgentTemplate("image-finish").fields, null, 2));'
```

Scaffold a recipe with a known template ID, then validate the resulting JSON. [Create your first recipe](docs/quickstart.md) walks through those steps. Unknown template IDs and settings are rejected; new capabilities require a reviewed source contribution following [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#new-reviewed-operations).

The [MCP adapter](docs/mcp.md) exposes all 39 template names. It prepares recipes by default and supports explicit local Ollama execution for the five writers. Canvas and vision execute through a browser host. Sharing source or importing recipe JSON does not create a public catalog listing; see [release and review](docs/release-and-feature.md).

<!-- docs/runtimes.md -->

### Runtimes and model setup

Choose the runtime for the result you need. The canvas SDK runs without a model or external dependency. Vision, tracking and browser writing use reviewed optional model runtimes. Interactive scenes and avatars use the shared Three.js engine. Node writing uses your own installed Ollama service. Guided recipes prepare direction for a separate host workflow.

The examples below use relative imports from an entry file at the cloned repository root. An application can bundle these source modules or use the exported package entry points through a local source dependency; the package is not distributed on npm yet. For a working model-free browser workspace, see [examples/browser](examples/browser/README.md).

| Runtime | Setup | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Canvas](docs/runtimes.md#canvas-processing) | Local browser; no model or dependency install | PNG images and design artboards |
| [Browser writing](docs/runtimes.md#browser-writing) | WebGPU, pinned WebLLM dependency, local worker and selected-agent model setup | Validated written documents |
| [Browser vision](docs/runtimes.md#browser-vision) | Pinned MediaPipe dependency, local WASM/worker and selected-agent model setup | Person cutout PNGs, pose or face landmarks |
| [Interactive 3D](docs/runtimes.md#interactive-3d-scenes) | Optional pinned Three.js; browser WebGL | Real scene preview, PNG and scene recipe |
| [Camera and avatar](docs/runtimes.md#camera-effects-and-face-driven-avatars) | Explicit camera permission; optional pinned face tracking worker | Canvas filters and original avatar rendering |
| [Local Ollama](docs/runtimes.md#local-ollama-writing) | Already running local service and installed eligible model | Validated written documents |
| [MCP](docs/mcp.md) | Node stdio adapter; Ollama only for explicit writing runs | Prepared recipes or local written results |

#### Canvas processing

Import the dependency-free engine from a local web page or bundler. Package consumers can import `@optimai/creative-agents/browser-runtime`; direct browser imports use `./src/browser-runtime.mjs`. No Studio account, credential, host application or network service is needed. The module does not touch browser APIs until you run an operation, so its pure size and validation helpers can also run in Node.

```js
import { runLocalTool, validateLocalImageFile } from './src/browser-runtime.mjs';

// Obtain this File from an <input type="file"> or a local drag-and-drop action.
const file = imageInput.files[0];
const error = validateLocalImageFile(file);
if (error) throw new Error(error);

const controller = new AbortController();
const result = await runLocalTool('image-resize', [file], {
  width: 1600, ratio: '16:9', fit: 'contain', background: '#101312'
}, controller.signal);

const url = URL.createObjectURL(result.blob);
preview.src = url;
download.href = url;
download.download = result.filename;
// Keep this URL until the preview is replaced or removed, then release it.
// URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
```

The engine accepts actual local `File` objects only. PNG, JPEG and WebP signatures are checked before decoding; URLs, SVG and other file formats are rejected. Each file and exported PNG is limited to 20 MiB, images to 4096 pixels on either side, and retained decoded images and output canvases to 16 million pixels. Image Grid supports up to eight files within that combined pixel limit; the other processors use one. The engine cleans up bitmap, canvas and temporary object URL resources on success, failure and cancellation. The consumer owns and must revoke any URL it creates from the returned Blob.

| Operation | Settings |
| --- | --- |
| `image-filter` | `preset`: original, noir, warm, cool or punchy; `intensity`: 0–100; `colorEngine`: pixel or css; `seed`: 0–4294967295 for grain ([pixel color grade](docs/runtimes.md#pixel-color-grade)); `film`: none, golden, teal-amber or matte; `lut`: `.cube` text ([LUTs and film looks](docs/runtimes.md#luts-and-film-looks)) |
| `image-resize` | `width`, `height`: positive integers up to 4096; `ratio`: original, 1:1, 16:9, 9:16 or 4:5; `fit`: cover or contain; `crop`: smart or center; `background`: hex color |
| `image-grid` | `columns`: 1–4; `gap`: 0–80 pixels; `crop`: smart or center; `background`: hex color |
| `type-overlay` | `title`: 1–300 characters; `fontSize`: 12–240; `color`: hex color; `position`: top, center or bottom; `ink`: readable, image or exact ([readable titles](docs/runtimes.md#readable-titles-and-image-palettes)) |

For a fixed resize ratio, width determines height when supplied; supplying only height determines width. With the original ratio, a single supplied side preserves the source proportions, while supplying both sides creates that exact canvas. The cover or contain setting determines how the image fits this canvas. Cover fits use [focus-aware cropping](docs/runtimes.md#focus-aware-cropping) unless `crop` is `center`. The color finish grades every pixel itself and needs no browser color-filter support. Rendering and PNG encoding run in the browser; Node tests use controlled canvas and image fixtures to verify the real exported engine, validation, geometry and resource cleanup.

##### Composition workspaces

```js
import { CANVAS_LAB_AGENTS, runCanvasLab } from './src/canvas-lab.mjs';

const controller = new AbortController();
const output = await runCanvasLab(CANVAS_LAB_AGENTS['poster-lab'], [], {
  title: 'EXPLORE\nSOMETHING NEW', color: '#c6f87d', ratio: '4:5', treatment: 'editorial'
}, controller.signal);
```

`mockup` creates a phone, desktop or gallery frame from one image. `bento` fits up to eight images into an asymmetric layout. `blend` and `transition` require exactly two images and use `mix: 0–100`; `transition` draws a real [still transition](docs/runtimes.md#still-transitions) at that time rather than a crossfade. `glitch` draws a [seeded glitch](docs/runtimes.md#seeded-glitch) on one still image with `amount: 0–100`, an `effect` and a `seed`. `print` turns one still image into a [print look](docs/runtimes.md#print-looks) with a `look`, `scale`, `amount`, `seed`, an ink `color` and riso `inks`. `poster` and `letter` accept one optional background image and a plain-text title of 1–180 characters. Ratios are 1:1, 4:5, 16:9 and 9:16; output width is 1200 pixels. Each image retains the signature and size checks of the original processor, and retained normalized inputs share a 16-million-pixel budget. Pending decode and export can be cancelled; late bitmaps and temporary canvases are disposed. Every image these compositions cover, crop or frame uses [focus-aware cropping](docs/runtimes.md#focus-aware-cropping); pass `crop: 'center'` for a classic centred fit. Poster and letter titles use [readable ink](docs/runtimes.md#readable-titles-and-image-palettes) by default; pass `ink: 'exact'` to draw `color` unchanged. Titles are set in [balanced lines](docs/runtimes.md#balanced-titles) with optical tracking and leading. These tools export PNGs, not video or model-generated artwork.

##### Focus-aware cropping

A cover fit can only slide its crop along one axis, so a centred crop often cuts off an off-centre subject. Each image is analysed once from a thumbnail of at most 96 pixels on its long side, about a millisecond of work on a recent laptop. Two signals are combined:

- **Detail**: Sobel gradient magnitude of luminance.
- **Distinctiveness**: OKLab distance from the image's mean color, after the frequency-tuned salient-region method of Achanta et al., 2009.

The crop then moves toward the window that holds the most interest near its centre. A small centre prior breaks ties. Transparent pixels score zero. The analysis has no model, network, face recognition or skin-tone heuristic. Flat images, matching aspect ratios and environments that cannot read canvas pixels keep the centred crop, so the result is never worse than a plain cover fit.

The same engine is available on its own for your own layouts:

```js
import { analyzeImageFocus, focusCoverRect } from './src/smart-crop.mjs';

const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(file);
const focus = analyzeImageFocus(bitmap, bitmap.width, bitmap.height); // null keeps a centred crop
const area = focusCoverRect(bitmap.width, bitmap.height, 1080, 1350, focus);
context.drawImage(bitmap, area.x, area.y, area.width, area.height, 0, 0, 1080, 1350);
```

`computeFocusMap(rgba, width, height)` and `findFocusCrop(map, width, height, aspect)` expose the pure steps, which also run in Node. Package consumers import `@optimai/creative-agents/smart-crop`.

##### Pixel color grade

Image Finish used to rely on the browser's canvas `filter`, which some browser versions lack, and there the presets silently did nothing. It now grades every pixel itself, in OKLab, so a finish looks the same in every browser and the same image, preset, intensity and seed always give identical bytes.

Each pixel goes from sRGB to linear light (exposure), then to OKLab, where the look is applied:

| Setting | Range (identity) | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exposure` | −2 to 2 stops (0) | Scales linear light. |
| `contrast` | −1 to 1 (0) | An S-curve on lightness through black, white and mid grey, so mid grey stays put. |
| `fade` | 0 to 0.3 (0) | Lifts the blacks. |
| `saturation` | 0 to 2 (1) | Scales chroma; 0 is monochrome. |
| `vibrance` | −1 to 1 (0) | Boosts muted colors more than vivid ones. |
| `temperature`, `tint` | −1 to 1 (0) | Shift along OKLab b (blue ↔ yellow) and a (green ↔ magenta), weighted by lightness so blacks stay neutral. |
| `shadowHue`/`shadowTint`, `highlightHue`/`highlightTint` | 0–360°, 0 to 0.1 (0) | Split toning: one hue pushed into the shadows, another into the highlights. |
| `grain` | 0 to 1 (0) | Seeded luminance grain, strongest in the midtones, keyed on pixel coordinates. |

The five presets (`original`, `noir`, `warm`, `cool`, `punchy`) are combinations of these settings; `intensity` scales every setting from the identity, so 0 is always the untouched image. Large images are graded in bands of rows and stay cancellable. `output.colorEngine` reports `pixel`. Pass `colorEngine: 'css'` for the previous filter look; it is also the fallback when a context cannot read its own pixels. Saved recipes need no new field.

The engine is a public module that runs on any RGBA buffer in Node and the browser:

```js
import { GRADE_PRESETS, gradeColor, gradePixels, resolveGrade } from '@optimai/creative-agents/color-grade';

const pixels = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height);
gradePixels(pixels.data, width, height, resolveGrade('warm', 0.6));                  // in place
gradePixels(pixels.data, width, height, resolveGrade({ fade: 0.08, grain: 0.3, shadowHue: 200, shadowTint: 0.03 }), { seed: 42 });
ctx.putImageData(pixels, 0, 0);
const swatch = gradeColor('#d8b48c', 'cool');                                         // preset chips and previews
```

`gradePixels(rgba, width, height, grade, { seed, rows })` grades in place and keeps alpha; `rows: [start, end)` grades one band with the same result as a single pass. `resolveGrade(presetOrSettings, amount)` validates and freezes a grade. Live camera effects still use the canvas filter.

##### LUTs and film looks

After the grade, Image Finish can apply a 3D lookup table: one of three original film looks (`film`: `golden`, `teal-amber` or `matte`) or a creator's own `.cube` file (`lut`: the file's text, which wins over `film`). `intensity` scales the LUT together with the grade, the look is applied in the same cancellable bands, and `output.lut` names what was applied. A look needs the pixel engine: with `colorEngine: 'css'`, or where a context cannot read its pixels, the run fails with a clear message instead of silently dropping the look. Both settings are engine-only, so saved recipes need no new field.

| Film | Character |
| --- | --- |
| `golden` | Warm highlights, slightly green-cool shadows, a gentle black lift and soft whites. |
| `teal-amber` | Teal-blue shadows and amber skin tones with stronger contrast. |
| `matte` | Lifted blacks, softened whites and muted color. |

The parser is strict and bounded: 3D tables only, `LUT_3D_SIZE` 2–65 before the table, optional `TITLE`, `DOMAIN_MIN`/`DOMAIN_MAX` (or `LUT_3D_INPUT_RANGE`) and `#` comments, exactly size³ rows of three numbers, and at most 16 MiB. 1D tables, unknown keywords, duplicates and stray rows are refused with the line number. Tables are indexed on encoded sRGB, red fastest, as grading tools export them; inputs outside the domain clamp to its edge.

```js
import { applyLut, createLut, filmLut, formatCubeLut, lutColor, parseCubeLut } from '@optimai/creative-agents/lut';

const lut = parseCubeLut(await file.text());                                          // throws with the line it refused
applyLut(pixels.data, width, height, lut, { amount: 0.8 });                           // trilinear, in place, alpha kept
const chip = lutColor('#c08060', filmLut('teal-amber'));                              // swatches for a film row
const cube = formatCubeLut(createLut(([r, g, b]) => [b, g, r], { size: 17, title: 'Swap' })); // bake and export your own
```

`applyLut(rgba, width, height, lut, { amount, rows })` gives identical bytes whole or band by band, and an identity table is lossless. `FILM_LOOKS` holds each film as a few numbers (gains, saturation, split tone, contrast, black and white points); `filmLut(name)` bakes it once into a shared 33³ table.

##### Readable titles and image palettes

A title color that reads on a dark photo can vanish on a bright one. Poster Lab, Letter Pose and Title Frame sample the composition behind the title block (a thumbnail of at most 64 pixels), find its dominant colors, and check the ink against every color that covers at least 5% of that area. The `ink` setting chooses what happens:

| `ink` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `readable` (default) | Keep `color` when it reaches 3:1 WCAG contrast (AA for large text) over each of those colors. When a small lightness move is enough, move only its OKLCH lightness, by the smallest step that passes, so the hue the creator chose survives. When it would take a big move (white turning grey over a bright sky), keep the color and draw the lightest scrim that passes behind the title instead; see [calm title placement](docs/runtimes.md#calm-title-placement). `scrim: 'off'` always moves the lightness. |
| `image` | Start from the photo's accent (its most vivid color that is also present), then apply the same check. Falls back to `color`. |
| `exact` | Draw `color` unchanged, as before. |

The result reports the ink actually drawn as `output.ink`, so a host can say so ("Ink adjusted to #5c8300 to stay readable"). Title Frame also draws its outline on the far side of the background: a light halo behind a title darker than the image. Environments that cannot read canvas pixels draw `color` unchanged. Saved recipes need no new field.

The color engine is a public module that runs in Node and the browser:

```js
import { analyzeImageColors, mixColors, pickAccentColor, pickLegibleColor } from '@optimai/creative-agents/color';

const palette = analyzeImageColors(bitmap, bitmap.width, bitmap.height); // [{ color, weight, oklch }], or null
const accent = pickAccentColor(palette ?? []);                           // '#2452c4', or null for a neutral image
const behind = analyzeImageColors(canvas, canvas.width, canvas.height, { region: { x: 96, y: 1100, width: 1008, height: 260 } });
const { color, contrast, passes } = pickLegibleColor(behind, { prefer: [accent, '#c6f87d'], minContrast: 4.5 });
const hover = mixColors(color, '#ffffff', 0.2);                          // mixed in OKLab
```

| Export | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `toOklab`, `toOklch`, `fromOklab`, `fromOklch` | Conversions after [Björn Ottosson's OKLab](https://bottosson.github.io/posts/oklab/). Out-of-gamut colors keep lightness and hue and lose chroma. |
| `parseHexColor`, `formatHexColor` | `#rgb`/`#rrggbb` ↔ `[r, g, b]`. Every function takes either form and returns `#rrggbb`. |
| `mixColors(a, b, amount)` | Perceptual mix in OKLab: black and white mix to a true mid-grey, red and blue stay colorful. |
| `contrastRatio`, `relativeLuminance` | WCAG 2.x, shared with [tier-0 verification](docs/runtimes.md#tier-0-verification). Use these for conformance. |
| `lightnessContrast(text, background)` | A polarity-aware OKLab lightness difference on an Lc-like −100…100 scale, positive for dark text on a light background. It is a simple ranking aid, not APCA. |
| `pickLegibleColor(backgrounds, { prefer, minContrast })` | Tries each preferred color in order, keeps it or moves its lightness the least distance that passes over every background. With no passing option (black *and* white behind the text) it returns the strongest candidate, often a mid-tone, with `passes: false`: add a scrim. |
| `dominantColors(rgba, width, height, { count })` | Weighted k-means in OKLab over a 15-bit histogram with deterministic seeding, so the same pixels always give the same palette. Alpha weights each pixel. At most 262,144 pixels and 12 colors. |
| `pickAccentColor(palette)` | The swatch with the highest chroma × √weight, or null below `minChroma`. |
| `analyzeImageColors(source, width, height, { region, count })` | Palette of an image, video frame or canvas (or a region of it) from a 64-pixel thumbnail; null when pixels cannot be read. |

##### Balanced titles

Poster Lab, Letter Pose and Title Frame set their titles with a line breaker instead of first-fit wrapping. At the largest size that fits, the title keeps the fewest lines it needs, and the words are spread across those lines so they are as even as possible: no long first line over a lone last word. Hard line breaks in the title are kept. A title shrinks before any word is split between characters, and Poster Lab and Letter Pose shrink a long title rather than dropping its last lines. Type is optically sized: tracking tightens from +0.01em at 16px to −0.02em at 128px and leading from 1.25 to 1.08, so large titles sit tight and small ones stay open. `output.lines` reports the lines as drawn. Saved recipes need no new field.

The typesetter is a public module that works with any measure function, in Node or the browser:

```js
import { breakLines, canvasMeasure, fitTitle, opticalSize } from '@optimai/creative-agents/typeset';

const measure = canvasMeasure(context, size => `800 ${size}px Inter, system-ui`);
const title = fitTitle('Make something remarkable for the people you love', { measure, width: 900, height: 500, maxSize: 160, maxLines: 4 });
context.font = `800 ${title.fontSize}px Inter, system-ui`;
context.letterSpacing = `${title.tracking}px`;
title.lines.forEach((line, index) => context.fillText(line, 60, 80 + index * title.lineHeight));
```

`breakLines(text, { measure, width, fontSize, wrap, tracking })` breaks at one size. `wrap` is `balance` (default: the minimum number of lines, every line as even as possible), `pretty` (paragraph style: even lines and a free last line, but never a lone short word) or `greedy` (first fit). It is a small dynamic program over whole words, the idea behind Knuth–Plass line breaking without hyphenation. `fitTitle` searches sizes from `maxSize` down to `minSize`, measures each word and character once, and reports `fits: false` when nothing fits and `split: true` when a word had to be broken. `opticalSize(fontSize)` returns the tracking (em) and leading it uses; pass `tracking` or `leading` to override them.

##### Calm title placement

Poster Lab and Letter Pose place their titles with `position: 'auto'` by default: the title block goes to the calmest part of the composed image instead of over the subject. The smart-crop focus map of the composition (the same 96-pixel analysis used for cropping) is turned into a summed-area table, and the block is scored at a grid of spots inside the frame, below the credit line. Each spot's score is the interest under the block plus a little breathing room, relative to the image's average, plus a gentle cost for leaving the layout's usual spot (bottom for Poster Lab, centre for Letter Pose). The title moves only when the new spot is clearly calmer (by a quarter of the image's average interest), so a flat, evenly busy or ambiguous image keeps the classic layout. Left-aligned compositions can also move sideways. The Poster Lab shade follows a title that moved to the top; otherwise it darkens the bottom as before. A blank artboard, an image whose pixels cannot be read, and the fixed `top`, `center` and `bottom` positions never search.

Title Frame keeps its `position` field (`bottom` by default) and also accepts `position: 'auto'`.

A scrim is drawn only when the chosen ink still fails 3:1 contrast where the title landed and a small lightness move would not fix it: a soft rounded panel, black behind light ink and white behind dark ink, at the lowest opacity (in 1% steps, from 15% so it is never invisibly faint, up to 60%) that passes over every color behind the title. If even that falls short, the ink also moves over what the scrim leaves. `output.placement` (`{ position, x, y, moved }`) and `output.scrim` (`{ color, opacity }` or null) report what was drawn; `scrim: 'off'` and `ink: 'exact'` keep the earlier behaviour. Saved recipes need no new field.

The placement steps are a public module that runs in Node and the browser:

```js
import { analyzeImageFocus } from '@optimai/creative-agents/smart-crop';
import { chooseTitleInk, placeTextBlock } from '@optimai/creative-agents/text-placement';

const focus = analyzeImageFocus(canvas, canvas.width, canvas.height);
const place = placeTextBlock(focus, { canvas, block: { width: title.width, height: title.height }, bounds: { x: 60, y: 120, width: 960, height: 1200 }, home: { x: 0, y: 1 } });
const { ink, scrim } = chooseTitleInk(backgroundsUnder(place), { prefer: ['#ffffff'], minContrast: 3 });
```

`placeTextBlock` also takes `homeBias` (default 0.25, in units of average interest), `minGain` (default 0.25), `columns`, `rows` (at most 33 each) and `breathing` (pixels, default 4% of the shorter side), and returns `interest` and `homeInterest` so you can explain a move. `regionInterest(focus, rect, canvas)` scores any rectangle, and `fitScrim(backgrounds, ink, { minContrast, minOpacity, maxOpacity, color })` returns the lightest scrim on its own, with the backgrounds as seen through it.

##### Still transitions

Transition Lab draws one frame of a move between two shots at `mix` (0–100, the time through the move) and a strip of the whole move. `transition` picks the move: `wipe` (a feathered edge travelling in `direction`: `right`, `left`, `down` or `up`), `radial` (an iris opening from the centre), `luma` (the brightest parts of the first shot give way first, like light burning through), `push` (both shots slide together in `direction`) or `dissolve`. The recipe's technique names are aliases: *match cut* draws `radial`, *camera move* `push`, *light wipe* `wipe` and *morph* `luma`. `pace` sets the feathered edge (`quick` 4%, `gentle` 15%, `slow cinematic` 35% of the move) and time is eased in and out, so the default middle frame is the true midpoint and evenly spaced frames read as motion. Frame 0 is exactly the first shot and frame 100 exactly the second.

`frames` (default 5; 0, or 2–12) sets the strip: one PNG of evenly spaced frames, each at most 320 pixels wide. The result adds `output.transition` (`{ style, direction, pace, progress }`, with `requested` when a canvas that cannot read its pixels fell back to a dissolve) and `output.strip` (`{ blob, width, height, frames }`, where `frames` lists each frame's time in percent, or null). A dissolve needs no pixel reads. Reference Blend keeps its plain `mix` crossfade, and saved recipes need no new field. The run itself is a still preview; for a video of the whole move, `createTransitionClip` draws each frame for [video export](docs/host-integration.md#export-video-with-webcodecs-or-the-recorder).

The compositor is a public module that works on any RGBA buffers in Node and the browser:

```js
import { composeTransition, resolveTransition, transitionProgress, transitionTimes } from '@optimai/creative-agents/transition';

const plan = resolveTransition({ style: 'wipe', direction: 'left', pace: 'gentle' });
const frame = composeTransition(first.data, second.data, width, height, transitionProgress(0.4, plan.ease), plan);
const times = transitionTimes(8);                                                    // 0, 1/7 … 1 for a contact sheet
```

`resolveTransition` also takes `ease` (`linear`, `in-out` or `out`), `softness` (0 for a hard edge, up to 1) and `center` (`[x, y]` fractions, to open an iris on a subject). Every style but `push` can write into one of its inputs; the output is opaque.

##### Seeded glitch

Glitch Cut draws a still-image glitch from a seed, so a shared recipe brings back the exact same picture. `effect` picks the look: `blocks` (shifted row bands and shuffled blocks), `trails` (a wide RGB split smeared into colour trails) or `echoes` (faint offset copies and deeper scanlines). The recipe's treatment names are aliases: *block displacement* draws `blocks`, *colour trails* `trails` and *frame echoes* `echoes`. `amount` (0–100, default 35) scales every part of it, and 0 is the untouched image. `seed` (a whole number from 0 to 999999, default 1) is a recipe field: the same image, effect, amount and seed give identical bytes on every engine, and another seed gives another arrangement. It is a still effect and never flashes.

The result adds `output.glitch` (`{ effect, seed, amount, engine }`). `engine` is `pixels` for the full glitch, or `bands` where a canvas cannot read its pixels: then only the seeded band shifts and a soft tint are drawn, still reproducible from the seed.

The glitch is a public module that works on any RGBA buffer in Node and the browser:

```js
import { glitchPixels, planGlitch, randomGlitchSeed } from '@optimai/creative-agents/glitch';

const seed = randomGlitchSeed();                                        // keep it to reproduce this look
const plan = planGlitch(width, height, { effect: 'trails', amount: 60, seed });
glitchPixels(image.data, width, height, plan, image.data);              // in place
```

`planGlitch` returns the layout (row `bands` with their `shift`, `blocks` with their move, the RGB `split`, `scanlines` and `echoes`) so a host can explain or animate it. `mulberry32(seed)` is the generator underneath, and `resolveGlitch` validates settings on their own. The plan uses only the generator and basic arithmetic, never `Math.sin` or other functions whose last bit can differ between engines.

##### Print looks

Print Shop prints one still image on warm paper (`#f4efe6`). `look` picks the process:

| `look` | Recipe name | What it draws |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `riso` | *riso duotone* | The image separated into two inks (`inks`: *pink + blue*, *orange + teal*, *yellow + purple* or *red + black*), each laid down as blue-noise grain and multiplied on the paper, with the first ink a few pixels off register |
| `halftone` | *halftone dots* | Round dots on a 45° screen, sized by each cell's mean tone; past 50% the paper shows through as round holes |
| `floyd-steinberg` | *error diffusion* | Floyd–Steinberg error diffusion, serpentine so the error never streaks one way |
| `bayer` | *ordered dither* | An 8 × 8 Bayer threshold: the crisp crosshatch of early screens |
| `blue-noise` | *blue-noise grain* | A 64 × 64 void-and-cluster threshold tile: even grain without a visible pattern |

The one-color looks print in `color` (default `#1f2433`). `scale` (1–12, default 3) is the dither cell in pixels; halftone cells are four times larger. `amount` (0–100, default 100) mixes the print over the original, and 0 is the untouched image. `seed` (0–999999, default 1) moves and turns the blue-noise tile and sets the riso misregistration: the same image and settings give identical bytes on every engine. Tones are stretched between their 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles first, so flat photos still print with a full range, and midtones are then lightened as prepress does for dot gain (`dotGain`, 0–1, default 0.45: coverage becomes x·(1 − g) + x²·g; 0 prints tones linearly), so a moody photo still shows its faces. A print needs pixel reads: on a canvas that cannot read them, Print Shop fails with a clear message rather than exporting the unprinted image. The result adds `output.print` (`{ look, scale, amount, seed, inks | ink, paper }`).

The looks are a public module that works on any RGBA buffer in Node and the browser:

```js
import { printPixels, separateDuotone, blueNoiseMatrix } from '@optimai/creative-agents/print';

printPixels(image.data, width, height, { look: 'riso', inks: 'orange + teal', seed: 7 }, image.data); // in place
printPixels(image.data, width, height, { look: 'halftone', scale: 4, ink: '#102030' }, image.data);
const [pink, blue] = separateDuotone([180, 90, 140], '#ff48b0', '#0078bf');                       // ink coverages, 0–1
```

`bayerMatrix(size)` and `blueNoiseMatrix(size)` return the threshold ranks for your own shaders, and `resolvePrint` validates settings on their own. Every look uses integer math, basic arithmetic and `Math.sqrt` only; the blue-noise tile is built once from integer weights, so it does not depend on the last bit of `Math.exp`.

##### Tier-0 verification

Before paying a model to judge a draft, an agent can reject the obviously broken ones locally. `@optimai/creative-agents/verify` provides deterministic checks with no model, network or dependency. They run in Node and the browser in milliseconds:

| Check | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `checkTextContrast` | The 5th-percentile WCAG contrast of known-color text over the pixels behind it reaches `minRatio` (4.5 by default; 3 for large text). A low percentile, not the mean, so a busy background cannot hide. |
| `checkTextSize` | Rendered text is at least `minPx` tall. |
| `checkTextOverlap` | Text boxes cover at most `maxShare` of the image's visual interest, measured on the focus map above. |
| `checkSafeZone`, `checkAspect`, `checkDuration`, `checkCount` | Boxes stay inside the safe zone; the delivered size, duration and detector count are within bounds. |
| `checkPalette` | Enough opaque pixels are within `maxDeltaE` of a brand color in OKLab. |
| `checkCutAlignment` | Enough edit cuts land within `tolerance` seconds of a beat, from any beat tracker. |

```js
import { computeFocusMap } from './src/smart-crop.mjs';
import { checkTextContrast, checkTextOverlap, summarizeChecks } from './src/verify.mjs';

const { data } = context.getImageData(0, 0, 96, 120); // a thumbnail of the poster
const headline = { x: 0.08, y: 0.06, width: 0.84, height: 0.14 };
const summary = summarizeChecks([
  checkTextContrast(data, 96, 120, headline, [255, 255, 255]),
  checkTextOverlap({ map: computeFocusMap(data, 96, 120), width: 96, height: 120 }, [headline]),
]);
if (!summary.pass) console.log('Regenerate before judging:', summary.failed);
```

Every result is `{ check, pass, score, threshold, confidence, costMs }`. Scores are oriented so that higher is better and `pass` means `score >= threshold`, so a host can calibrate any score into a probability with one monotone fit. `confidence` is a margin from the threshold (0.5–1), not a probability. Pass thumbnails: pixel checks read at most 262,144 pixels.

To execute a saved composition recipe, normalize its fields before rendering:

```js
import { canvasLabRecipeSettings, runCanvasLab } from './src/canvas-lab.mjs';

const settings = canvasLabRecipeSettings('poster-lab', {
  title: 'A NEW PERSPECTIVE', format: 'wide banner', style: 'cinematic'
});
const output = await runCanvasLab(settings.operation, [], settings, controller.signal);
```

The normalizer merges source defaults, maps legacy poster `format` to `ratio`, letter `text` to `title`, `style` to `treatment`, glitch `intensity` to `amount`, glitch treatment names to `effect` and print style names to `look`. Explicit canonical values win. It validates recipe values and the final engine settings. Do not merge defaults into supplied values before calling it: that would conceal whether a canonical setting was explicitly selected. Raw `runCanvasLab` remains available for applications using direct bounded engine settings.

#### Selected-agent model setup

`getModelSetupPolicy(model, environment)` is a pure public policy: it never fetches a model, starts a worker or asks for camera permission. A host applies it when the user opens a model-backed agent, then calls the reviewed download/load API in code. This keeps preparation convenient while making size, progress, cancellation and retry visible.

```js
import { getModelSetupPolicy } from './src/model-setup.mjs';
import { VISION_MODELS, loadVisionModelBuffer } from './src/vision-runtime.mjs';
import { describeProgress } from './src/progress.mjs';

const policy = getModelSetupPolicy(VISION_MODELS['face-reference'], {
  browser: true, webGPU: Boolean(navigator.gpu),
  saveData: navigator.connection?.saveData,
  effectiveType: navigator.connection?.effectiveType,
  deviceMemory: navigator.deviceMemory
});
// Always show policy.reason, model size, progress and a Stop control in the host.
if (policy.mode === 'automatic') {
  const bytes = await loadVisionModelBuffer('face-reference', {
    signal: controller.signal, onProgress: progress => showProgress(describeProgress(progress)) // "Downloading 1.2 MB of 3.8 MB · 32%"
  });
  // Pass these owned verified bytes to the reviewed local tracking worker.
}
// manual: display Download and let that click call the same preparation API.
// unsupported: keep basic filters, procedural demos, canvas tools or guided direction available.
```

Data Saver and 2G connections use manual setup. Large models also use manual setup on 3G or when reported device memory is below 4 GB. A required but unavailable WebGPU environment is unsupported. Automatic mode prepares only the selected reviewed model; it does not download every catalog model. The host still performs capability checks beyond this coarse policy. Cancel preparation when a workspace closes, preserve its user's input and offer a deliberate retry; cancel is not permission to restart a download automatically.

##### Setup controller and sizes

`createModelSetupController({ load, check, cancel, bytes, name, policy })` runs the visible setup flow so every host shows the same states: `idle → checking → downloading (loaded, total) → verifying → ready`, or `failed` / `unsupported`. It never fetches by itself. `load({ signal, onProgress })` is your reviewed call (`downloadVisionModel`, browser writer `load()`…), and the optional `check({ signal })` returns `{ ready, available, loading, cached, message }`.

```js
import { createModelSetupController, describeModelSetup, getModelSetupPolicy } from './src/model-setup.mjs';
import { BROWSER_AGENT_MODEL } from './src/browser-writing-runtime.mjs';

const size = describeModelSetup(BROWSER_AGENT_MODEL); // { download: '453 MB', memory: 'about 1.7 GB GPU memory', label }
const setup = createModelSetupController({
  name: 'writing AI', bytes: BROWSER_AGENT_MODEL.downloadBytes,
  policy: () => getModelSetupPolicy({ bytes: BROWSER_AGENT_MODEL.downloadBytes, requiresWebGPU: true }, readEnvironment()),
  check: async () => ({ ...await runtime.status(), cached: await isCached() }),
  load: ({ signal, onProgress }) => runtime.load({ signal, onProgress }),
  cancel: () => runtime.cancel(),
});
setup.subscribe(state => render(state.state, state.progress, state.progressLabel)); // "120 MB of 453 MB"
await setup.check({ autoStart: true }); // ready, unsupported, observes a load already running, or starts when cached/automatic
stopButton.onclick = () => setup.abort(); // back to idle; late progress from the stopped run is ignored
```

The state object is frozen and replaced on every change, so `subscribe`/`getState` work directly with React's `useSyncExternalStore`. Progress accepts `{ stage | phase, loaded, total, progress, message }`: a fraction is converted to bytes with the declared `bytes`, a reported `total` replaces it, and bytes never move backwards within one run. A `verify` stage becomes `verifying`. A second `start()` joins the running one, a user's `start()` or `abort()` during `check()` wins over the late check result, and a check that finds a load already running polls it (`pollMs`, default 800) instead of starting a duplicate download; `abort()` then calls your `cancel`. `reset({ state, message })` resyncs after the model was released elsewhere. With a `check`, the controller starts in `checking` so no Download button flashes before the first check; `policy` may be a function so browser hints are read at check time rather than during server rendering; `dispose()` on unmount stops only this controller's own download and polling, never a load it merely observed. `formatBytes` uses decimal units as operating systems show downloads (`453 MB`, `3.8 MB`, `1.7 GB`), and `describeModelProgress({ loaded, total })` gives `"120 MB of 453 MB"`.

`downloadVisionModel`, `loadVisionModelBuffer` and browser writer `load()` remain explicit function calls internally. Recipes contain neither download policy nor model/worker URLs. Inference stays separate from setup: preparing a model does not generate a new take, request a camera or trigger paid production.

#### Browser writing

Install the reviewed optional dependency in your isolated browser host:

```sh
npm install --save-exact @mlc-ai/web-llm@0.2.85
```

Create a local worker entry that imports `WebWorkerMLCEngineHandler` from the installed WebLLM dependency and calls the kit's `attachBrowserWritingWorker(WebWorkerMLCEngineHandler)`. Bundle that entry locally; a recipe cannot supply its own worker URL. The runtime downloads only the configured public Qwen 3.5 0.8B model and matching compiled WebGPU library when the host calls `load()`, either automatically after agent selection under the setup policy or through a manual Download control. The first download is approximately **453.2 MB**; HTTPS or localhost, Web Workers, WebGPU with `shader-f16` and sufficient GPU memory are required. The configured context is 4096 tokens, and the official model estimate is approximately 1.63 GB of GPU memory. Device support checks are conservative and cannot guarantee successful allocation on every GPU.

```js
import { createBrowserAgentRuntime } from './src/browser-writing-runtime.mjs';

const controller = new AbortController();
const writer = createBrowserAgentRuntime({
  createWorker: () => new Worker(new URL('./writing-worker.mjs', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }),
  loadEngine: () => import('@mlc-ai/web-llm')
});
const support = await writer.status(); // No engine or model download.
if (!support.available) throw new Error(support.message);
await writer.load({ signal: controller.signal }); // Host calls this after the setup policy permits preparation.
const draft = await writer.run({
  templateId: 'story-seed', brief: 'An explorer helps a lost cloud.',
  values: { form: 'manga', style: 'manga' }, signal: controller.signal
});
console.log(draft.sections); // Plain untrusted text; never raw HTML.
```

The host's `writing-worker.mjs` contains only the reviewed SDK wiring:

```js
import { WebWorkerMLCEngineHandler } from '@mlc-ai/web-llm';
import { attachBrowserWritingWorker } from './src/browser-writing-worker.mjs';
attachBrowserWritingWorker(WebWorkerMLCEngineHandler);
```

The five writing contracts are Cast Notes, Style Brief, Storyboard Builder, Prompt Branches and Story Seed. Briefs are limited to 2,000 characters in the browser, with a 2,048-token output budget. New storyboards start with three scenes for a quick draft. Longer storyboards can take several minutes on a compact model. Storyboards longer than three scenes are written scene by scene with preceding actions as continuity context, then the combined artifact is validated. A malformed or incomplete draft receives one bounded repair; failure is reported without substituting a canned document. `cancel()` terminates the active worker, and `unload()` releases the session. Model files are fetched and cached, while creative prompts and generated text remain in the browser. There is no server or Ollama fallback in this browser engine.

The model weights are pinned to Hugging Face commit `0ec138972555613c1d7812a821778ad0398c8790`; the compiled library is pinned to commit `025bcaf3780fa8254f5e5efd3bfea0a5397248f4`. Config, tokenizer files and compiled library use fixed integrity checks. WebLLM does not provide a per-shard integrity check for all weights, so the kit does not claim that guarantee. The WebLLM library and Qwen weights retain their upstream Apache-2.0 licenses; the kit's MIT license does not replace them.

#### Browser vision

Install the reviewed optional dependency in your isolated browser host:

```sh
npm install --save-exact @mediapipe/tasks-vision@1.1.0
```

Bundle a local worker that imports the MediaPipe namespace and calls `installVisionWorker(vision)` from `src/vision-processor.mjs`. Copy the official `vision_wasm_module_internal.js` and `.wasm` files into the host's local static assets, and supply their same-origin directory as `wasmBaseUrl`. No worker, executable URL or WASM path is taken from a recipe. The host is responsible for serving reviewed dependency assets and retaining their upstream licenses.

```js
import { downloadVisionModel, runBrowserVision } from './src/vision-runtime.mjs';

const controller = new AbortController();
const file = imageInput.files[0]; // A local file selected by the user.
await downloadVisionModel('person-cutout', { signal: controller.signal }); // Host policy or manual Download action.
const result = await runBrowserVision('person-cutout', file, {
  background: 'transparent', threshold: .5, softness: .12
}, {
  workerFactory: () => new Worker(new URL('./vision-worker.mjs', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }),
  wasmBaseUrl: new URL('./vision-wasm/', location.href).href,
  signal: controller.signal
});
console.log(result.blob, result.analysis);
```

Person Cutout uses Selfie Segmenter (249,537 bytes) for people in portrait photos. Motion Pose uses Pose Landmarker Lite (5,777,746 bytes) for one person's 33 body landmarks. Face Performance uses Face Landmarker (3,758,596 bytes) for one visible face's 478 landmarks and raw blendshape coefficients. It does not identify people, infer personality or emotions, or swap faces. Model URLs are fixed official Google storage version-1 assets and checked against exact byte lengths and SHA-256 hashes. `getVisionModelStatus()` reads local cache only; `runBrowserVision()` never implicitly downloads a model. `loadVisionModelBuffer()` returns owned verified bytes and can prepare a missing model when `downloadIfMissing: true`; use `false` for cache-only access.

Vision progress events use the shared [progress shape](docs/host-integration.md#show-staged-progress-with-one-event-shape): `stage` is download, verify, ready, prepare, warmup, analyze or render, downloads carry `loaded`/`total` bytes, and the older `phase` field is kept (`initialize` there is `warmup`).

Vision requires HTTPS or localhost, Web Crypto, Web Workers, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas and WASM SIMD support. It uses a CPU worker and does not require WebGPU. Check the target browser before enabling the workspace.

Selected PNG, JPEG and WebP images remain in the browser. Inputs are limited to 20 MiB, 4096 pixels per side and 16 million pixels; analysis and PNG output are scaled to at most 1600 pixels per side. A CPU WASM worker is stopped after 60 seconds or on cancellation. Results depend on subject visibility and the model's training scope; an undetected subject produces a useful error rather than a fabricated landmark result. Raw landmark analysis is available in `result.analysis`; the consumer can create a reviewed JSON export if needed.

#### Interactive 3D scenes

Install the optional reviewed peer in the host: `npm install --save-exact three@0.186.1`. TypeScript hosts can install `@types/three@0.186.0` for its declarations. Nothing is fetched by the scene engine itself. Public entry points are `scene-3d` for pure input/settings helpers and `scene-3d-runtime` for the browser renderer. The root manifest entry does not import Three.js.

```js
import { scene3DRecipeSettings } from './src/scene-3d.mjs';
import { createScene3DStage } from './src/scene-3d-runtime.mjs';

const recipe = scene3DRecipeSettings('scene-lighting', {
  demo: 'architecture', lighting: 'sunset', finish: 'original',
  view: 'iso', focalLength: 50, exposure: 120
});
const stage = await createScene3DStage(mountedContainer, recipe.settings, {
  signal: controller.signal, onError: message => showError(message)
});
stage.camera(recipe.camera);
// A selected self-contained file only; never pass a URL.
await stage.importGLB(await glbInput.files[0].arrayBuffer(), glbInput.files[0].name);
const png = await stage.png();
const recipeJson = stage.configuration();
// Call stage.dispose() on route/dialog close; this releases GPU objects and controls.
```

`createScene3DStage()` loads the installed optional peer only when called. A host that already bundles reviewed Three modules can avoid another module loading boundary with synchronous `createScene3DStageWithRuntime(container, settings, onError, { THREE, OrbitControls, GLTFLoader, RoomEnvironment })`. `loadScene3DRuntime()` exposes the same optional peer loader. The [interactive example](examples/interactive/README.md) demonstrates local dependency injection.

The controller supports `update(settings)`, `demo('sculpture'|'product'|'architecture')`, `camera('isometric'|'front'|'side'|'top')`, `fit()`, `zoom('in'|'out')`, `importGLB(bytes, name)`, `png()`, `configuration()` and `dispose()`. Procedural demos contain original sculpture, headphone and architectural geometry. Materials can remain original or use ceramic, metal or clay; light presets are studio, sunset and neon. Lens controls use real 24–100 mm focal lengths. A portable recipe uses `finish`, `view` and exposure in 25–200 percent; `scene3DRecipeSettings` maps them to material, camera and renderer settings. Saved free-text subject/material fields remain compatible.

`validateAgentGLB()` runs before the glTF loader. It accepts one static embedded scene up to 20 MiB with 300,000 visible vertices, 128 primitives and 256 nodes. It validates accessor storage, indices, finite coordinates and a usable visible scene. Up to eight embedded PNG/JPEG images share a 16-megapixel budget and a 4096-pixel side limit. External/data URLs, compressed decoders, instancing, skins, morph targets and animations are rejected. A failed or late import preserves the prior scene or releases its unused result.

The renderer caps pixel density, renders manual previews only on change, and suspends turntable motion when hidden, offscreen or reduced motion is requested. Exports render the current camera immediately before PNG readback. The scene recipe contains settings and camera state; imported GLB geometry is not included. Keep the original model with it. `dispose()` releases geometry, material, textures, decoded bitmaps, environment/shadow targets, renderer and listeners. These ownership choices follow the [Three glTF loader's bitmap guidance](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/GLTFLoader.html); interaction uses [OrbitControls](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/OrbitControls.html).

#### Camera effects and face-driven avatars

`camera-runtime`, `camera-renderer`, `camera-tracking` and `camera-worker` are reusable public modules. They do not import Studio services. The host owns camera permission, selected media decoding, its render loop, snapshot/recording UI and any subsequent handoff. Basic clean/neon/prism/duotone/film canvas effects and the original avatar demo do not require a face-model download. Halo anchoring and face-driven avatar controls use a local Face Landmarker worker.

```js
import { cameraRecipeSettings, createCameraLease, createFaceRigSmoother, faceRigAt } from './src/camera-runtime.mjs';
import { createCameraAvatar, drawCameraEffect, drawFaceHalo } from './src/camera-renderer.mjs';
import { createFaceTracker } from './src/camera-tracking.mjs';
import { loadVisionModelBuffer } from './src/vision-runtime.mjs';

const settings = cameraRecipeSettings('avatar-stage', { look: 'orbit', mirror: 'yes' });
const bytes = await loadVisionModelBuffer('face-reference', { signal: controller.signal });
let latestFace = null;
const tracker = await createFaceTracker(bytes, {
  workerFactory: () => new Worker(new URL('./camera-worker.mjs', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }),
  wasmBaseUrl: new URL('./vision-assets/1.1.0', location.href).href,
  signal: controller.signal, onFace: frame => { latestFace = frame; }, onError: showError
});
const avatar = createCameraAvatar(avatarCanvas, settings.look, { THREE });
const lease = createCameraLease();
// Wire this to the user's Start camera button, not model preparation.
const stream = await lease.start(() => navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
  video: { width: { ideal: 1280 }, height: { ideal: 720 } }, audio: false
}));
if (stream) video.srcObject = stream;
// In your visible preview loop, first draw video into an unmirrored <=1280×720 input canvas:
tracker.submit(sourceCanvas, performance.now()); // At most one frame in flight; inference stays in worker.
const now = performance.now(); // Create one smoother per preview: const smoother = createFaceRigSmoother();
avatar.render(smoother.next(faceRigAt(latestFace, now, settings.mirror), now));
// Close/hidden/cancel: tracker.dispose(); avatar.dispose(); lease.close(); cancelAnimationFrame(loop);
```

The host's same-origin worker entry imports its locally served pinned MediaPipe bundle, then calls `installCameraWorker(vision)`. Use `loadVisionModelBuffer('face-reference')` to obtain cache-first verified bytes; the camera worker checks the exact model length and SHA-256 again before creating the task. `createFaceTracker` transfers ownership of the buffer to the worker. Worker and WASM paths are trusted host code; they must not come from recipe values. Its processing canvas is 640 × 360, face frames are compact, and the tracking pipeline keeps one bitmap/inference in flight at a 100 ms interval. Missing or stale faces return neutral rig values rather than retaining a previous person's motion.

`drawCameraSource` performs a cover crop; `drawCameraEffect` draws selected filters; `drawFaceHalo` draws landmark-aligned graphics. `faceRigFromFrame`, `faceRigAt` and `createFaceRigSmoother` map bounded transform/blendshape data into an original procedural avatar. Mirroring is applied after inference. Live camera access requires HTTPS/localhost and explicit browser permission, as documented by [getUserMedia](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getUserMedia).
